title: Notation, 32-bar form and piano method books
summary: Learning notation, how he explains 32-bar form to young players, and the John Thompson piano books.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: Did you find notating music hard for you, or did it come easily?

Well at first, until I really learned what it was all about. And I find it's much easier now than it was then, because I guess maybe the experiences have taught me a lot about it. And I pick it up and I know all about it right now. You see, whereas a young musician, I tell them, I say, play one chorus in a 32 bar song, they don't know what the heck I'm talking about. And I say, well man, look, I don't know what you had to teach him. I say, but in a 32 bar song, you got eight, eight, you know, in the air. You have two eights. Then an eight, another eight out. That's 32 bars. 32 bars. And you know, now I have this as a problem, because there's a lot of things that are 32 bar songs that we play. And I know it's, I'm telling the truth, because young musicians don't know nothing about it. I say, play one chorus. They don't know what I'm talking about. And then I have to, in turn, just lay it out in simple terms. Whereas with their music today, I know it, I listen to it, and I know all about it right off. But they didn't know nothing about just generally basic structure of music. Don't know.
So your piano teacher, what type of exercises did you have to do?

Well, we had books. We had the John Thompson. See, that's what we, the John Thompson was the book. See, we didn't use it. They had another book that most of the people that was, but in our school we used the John Thompson method, you know, the first, second, third level. And what happened? .
